Underlines why local-first coordination avoids flaky/remote MCP endpoints

stats.fact: The official MCP registry listed 18,849 servers (mid-2026), signaling broad MCP adoption.
Across 43,320 live probes of 9,326 remote MCP servers, 17.2% (1,603) are dead — they advertise an endpoint that does not answer.
Remote MCP servers have a median latency of ~233ms and ~27% hide their tooling behind auth.
Roundtable positions multi-agent (parallel specialized models) vs single-AI copy-paste as faster and less error-prone, with a single deterministic command.

angles: Local-first avoids dead/remote MCP servers: 17.2% of remote endpoints are dead, so keeping coordination local is more reliable.
Auditability as the differentiator: PeerBridge should log every agent-to-agent exchange locally for review and replay, unlike opaque remote orchestrators.
Peer model vs central controller: instead of a single orchestrator delegating, peers subscribe/publish over a local bus (Karpathy-style council), preserving context and session state.
No extra cloud infra: reuse existing CLI tools and local API subscriptions, keep all state on-disk (like ~/.agents-council/state.json).
Security: local-first reduces the prompt-injection/remote-tooling attack surface compared to connecting many remote MCP servers.
